questions.title: How does the 'fraudulent inducement' theory survive *Ciminelli*'s rejection of the 'right-to-control' theory in a social media pump-and-dump case?
questions.question_body: The district court dismissed the indictment arguing that the defendants only deprived victims of 'valuable economic information,' citing *United States v. Ciminelli*. However, the Fifth Circuit reversed, distinguishing between the 'right-to-control' theory (which *Ciminelli* killed) and the 'fraudulent-inducement' theory. I am struggling to understand exactly how the court distinguishes these two theories in practice. Specifically, if both involve deception leading to a financial decision, why does inducing someone to buy a stock (where they receive something of value in return) count as defrauding them of property under *Kousisis*, whereas withholding insider information does not? Is the critical distinction simply that one involves a direct transfer of money/property versus just a lost opportunity?

questions.title: Does *Kousisis* eliminate the requirement that a fraud defendant must intend to cause actual economic harm or loss to the victim?
questions.question_body: The defendants argued that their intent was merely to profit for themselves, not necessarily to harm their followers financially (since the followers received market-value securities after the 'pump'). The court cites *Kousisis* to say fraud statutes don't require a victim to suffer net pecuniary loss. This seems counter-intuitive: isn't fraud inherently about causing loss? If I trick you into buying a car worth $10k for $10k using lies about its color, but then sell it immediately for more than I paid, have I committed fraud if you didn't lose money? How does *Kousisis* redefine 'harm' in this context—is it purely about the unauthorized taking of possession/control rather than the final balance sheet outcome?

questions.title: What constitutes a 'material misrepresentation' in a social media pump-and-dump scheme where no physical asset changes hands initially?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that securities fraud requires a 'scheme to defraud' involving a material misrepresentation intended to deceive others into obtaining something of value. In this case, the defendants posted false info on social media about trading positions. My confusion lies in applying traditional fraud elements to digital content. Does posting a tweet constitute making a 'misrepresentation' in the same way as lying on a financial statement? Furthermore, since they alleged they profited $114 million from selling shares later ('dump'), does the misrepresentation need to directly relate to the specific transaction where money changed hands, or can it be general hype designed to move the market generally before any specific sale occurs?

questions.title: If an indictment relies on *Kousisis*, does it still need to explicitly allege that victims suffered an economic loss beyond just being induced to transact?
questions.question_body: Under Section II of this opinion, an indictment must '(2) fairly inform the defendant of the charges.' Given that *Kousisis* allows liability even when victims receive equivalent value (e.g., stocks bought at fair market price), what specific factual allegations must now be included in an indictment for securities fraud? Do prosecutors need to allege that victims were left with worthless paper after dumping occurred, or is it sufficient to merely allege that they were tricked into handing over money via false pretenses regarding their investment strategy? If they don't allege specific losses, will future indictments be vulnerable on double jeopardy grounds or failure-to-state-a-claim grounds similar to what happened here?

questions.title: How do courts reconcile the 'deception + obtaining property' test from *Ciminelli/Kousisis* with cases involving pure informational asymmetry?
questions.question_body: *Ciminelli* established that you can't prosecute someone for hiding information (right-to-control), while *Kousisis* confirms you can prosecute someone who actively lies (fraudulent inducement). In this case, defendants allegedly misrepresented their own trading positions and future price predictions. Where is the bright line between providing false opinions/predictions (which might be protected speech or non-actionable puffery) and actionable fraud? If I tell my Instagram followers 'This stock will go up tomorrow!' and it doesn't, is that different from telling them 'I own 50% of this company' when I actually own none? How does this opinion define where active deception ends and mere bad advice begins?
